$comment: APIM API AND BACKEND DEFINITIONS. What the policy files could not say.
The XML beside this file decides IDENTITY: it proves edge provenance, deletes every inbound
copy of the identity contract, validates the token once and states the closed X-Idp-* contract.
It cannot say which URL reaches which deployable, and until this file existed that routing lived
only in prose — specs/001-platform-scaffold/contracts/README.md and a sentence in tasks.md.
ROUTING IN PROSE IS ROUTING THAT IS SILENTLY WRONG. A misrouted /views path does not fail: it
reaches RagCore, which serves the audience but not that route, and returns a 404 that looks
exactly like a client calling something that does not exist. This file makes the routing table
a reviewable artifact and gives the validation tests something to check it against.
THE OPENAPI DOCUMENTS ARE GENERATED, NEVER HAND-WRITTEN (spec FR-DEMO-013, contracts README
rule 5). Every `openApi.source` below points at a document emitted from a RUNNING service —
FastAPI's schema for RagCore, the built-in generator for .NET Minimal APIs — and published by
.github/workflows/contracts.yml. A hand-maintained copy imported here would drift from what the
service accepts, and the drift would be invisible until a client believed the document.
ONE DOCUMENT PER AUDIENCE PER DEPLOYABLE, AND NEVER A MERGED ONE. A merged document would let a
customer-facing client discover the staff and workload surfaces, which is why the emission tasks
produce five documents rather than one.
$topology: client → Front Door + WAF → APIM → Container Apps (internal ingress) → RagCore / .NET
Each hop carries two independent controls, listed in build/policy/edge-trust.json. This file
configures the third hop's routing; it does not restate the controls.

$comment: MUTUAL TLS, AND IT IS A NAMED EXEMPTION RATHER THAN A PREFERENCE.
Managed identity is the platform default and is used for every Azure resource that
supports it (build/policy/azure-identity.json). It is not used on THIS hop, and the
reason is recorded as the one exemption in that file: what would validate a
managed-identity token at the ingress layer is Container Apps built-in authentication,
which is documented only for external ingress-enabled apps. These backends are
internal-only by design. Validating the token in application code instead is prohibited
by constitution Principle I — services MUST NOT parse an access token — so the choice is
between mutual TLS and giving the backends a JWT library, and the second one is worse.
WHAT IS ACTUALLY EXEMPTED IS NARROW. No component holds a standing secret: the private
key is in Key Vault, APIM reads it AS A MANAGED IDENTITY, and the backends hold only a
public SHA-256 hash. The exemption is not 'a credential lives outside the vault' — it is
that this credential has a lifecycle and an expiry, which a managed identity would not.
That residual is managed rather than accepted: rotation is a sequenced release and
expiry is alerted 45 days ahead.
Referenced by certificate-id and NEVER by thumbprint: a thumbprint changes on rotation
and a policy identifying it that way silently stops attaching a certificate at all.

backends.name: Integrations Service

$comment: THE SAME CERTIFICATE AND THE SAME RECORDED EXEMPTION as the other two backends. One
certificate rather than three: each backend validates the hash of the certificate APIM
presents, and three would triple the rotation surface for no gain - no backend needs to
tell APIM apart from APIM.
ROTATION ORDER IS THE CONTROL AND NOW SPANS THREE BACKENDS. Widen the allow-list on
every backend BEFORE repointing APIM (docs/runbooks/rotate-gateway-certificate.md). The
reverse order is a total outage on whichever backend was missed - and because health
probes are exempt from provenance, that backend stays green while serving nothing.
THE ONLY BACKEND THAT IS NOT CLIENT-FACING. No client calls it: only RagCore does, on the
workload audience, app-only, through APIM like any other caller (ADR-0007, spec 21.6).
It is also the only backend with an egress path to a customer system and the only holder of
the Key Vault role for connector credentials. Its ingress is internal-only for the same
reason as the others, but the consequence of getting that wrong is larger here: external
ingress would be a public route to the component holding every organisation's connector
secrets.

credentials.$comment: The same certificate and the same exemption. One certificate rather than two: the backends validate the hash of the certificate APIM presents, and two would double the rotation surface for no gain — neither backend needs to tell APIM apart from APIM.

$noSharedSecrets: NO BACKEND CREDENTIAL IN THIS FILE IS A SECRET, and none can be added.
APIM authenticates to a backend by presenting a certificate it reads from Key Vault as its own
managed identity. There is no authorization header value, no subscription key on a backend and
no shared key of any kind.
The forbidden credential shapes are enumerated in ONE place, build/policy/azure-identity.json,
and deliberately not repeated here. Two copies of a list like that drift, and the drift is
invisible until the weaker copy is the one somebody checked against.
list — including this file. It scans raw text, because JSON has no docstring for a scanner to
exclude, so a file explaining the rule by quoting it would trip it. That is a feature: it is
what makes the registry the single copy rather than the first of several.

$comment: Subscription keys are OFF, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. A subscription
key is a shared secret distributed to clients, and this platform authenticates callers with
an Entra token validated in the policy. Requiring both would add a credential that grants
nothing extra, cannot be attributed to a person, and would be the thing pasted into a
front-end bundle.
THE LONGEST MATCHING PATH WINS, and that is the whole routing rule for this audience:
/api/customer/v1/views/... reaches the monolith and everything else under
/api/customer/v1 reaches RagCore. APIM resolves the most specific prefix first, so the two
APIs coexist under one prefix without an ordering flag to get wrong.
SAME POLICY FILE AS THE API ABOVE, deliberately. Identity is derived per AUDIENCE, not per
deployable: a person is an end user on the customer surface whichever backend answers them.
Two policies here would be two places for the derivation to drift, and the drift would
appear as one backend seeing a role the other did not.
The monolith is READ-ONLY (ADR-0001), which is enforced at the platform rather than here:
its managed identity holds no Service Bus, SignalR, AI Search or model role at all.

$comment: NO VIEWS COUNTERPART, and that is a fact about the architecture rather than a gap. The
workload audience is the execution leg; the monolith is read-only and serves no execution
route. It is also the audience through which one service reaches another — app-only, and
through APIM like any other caller, because a direct pod-to-pod route MUST NOT exist
(contracts README rule 4).

$comment: THE LONGEST MATCHING PATH WINS, and that is the whole routing rule for this pair:
/api/workload/v1/integrations/... reaches the Integrations Service and everything else
under /api/workload/v1 reaches RagCore. APIM resolves the most specific prefix first, so
the two APIs coexist under one prefix with no ordering flag to get wrong. This is the same
idiom already proven by /api/customer/v1/views.
SAME POLICY FILE AS THE API ABOVE, deliberately. Identity is derived per AUDIENCE, not per
deployable: a caller is the workload principal whichever backend answers it. Two policies
here would be two places for the derivation to drift.
TWO DEPLOYABLES NOW EMIT A WORKLOAD DOCUMENT, and each emits its own. The rule is one
document per audience PER DEPLOYABLE (contracts README rule 5), so the compatibility gate
diffs per deployable rather than per audience. A merged document would let a
customer-facing client discover this surface.
REQUIRES A DISTINCT APPLICATION ROLE (workload.v1.xml). The generic workload role does not
grant access here: a component holding it must not be able to drive connectors merely by
being a workload caller.
THE RATE AND BUDGET BOUNDARY, at two levels that count different things.
GLOBAL, per IP (build/infra/apim/global.inbound.xml): bounds an anonymous flood before it
costs gateway capacity. It runs before any token is validated, which is exactly when it is
needed and exactly why it cannot be per-organisation — there is no organisation yet.
PER AUDIENCE, per ORGANISATION (the audience policy files): the control FR-OPS-005 actually
asks for. Counting by IP cannot do this job — one organisation behind one NAT is one IP and
fifty users of another are fifty — so it throttles the wrong callers and protects nobody from
a noisy neighbour.
The counter key is the DERIVED X-Idp-Tenant-Id, which is why the policy sits after identity
derivation. A budget keyed on anything a caller supplies is a budget a caller escapes by
changing it.
A THROTTLE IS NOT A FAILURE (FR-OPS-006). The user is told the request was limited.
The values are named values rather than literals: they are tuned per environment, and a
limit a deployment cannot adjust is one that gets removed entirely the first time it bites.

tokenBudget.$comment: Model spend is metered and budgeted separately, at the AI Gateway, on the same per-organisation key. Two resources, two meters, deliberately not merged: request volume and token spend fail for different reasons and at different rates.

$comment: Resolved at deployment. NONE is a credential: two are internal URLs, one is a certificate
ENTITY id (not the certificate), and the rest are numbers.
The backend URLs are internal Container Apps addresses. Knowing one grants nothing — ingress
is internal-only and requires a client certificate, so an attacker who learns the address
still has no way to reach it.

ragcore-backend-url.why: The internal ingress address of the RagCore container app.

monolith-backend-url.why: The internal ingress address of the monolith container app.

integrations-backend-url.why: The internal ingress address of the Integrations Service container app.

integrations-app-role.why: The application role a caller must hold to reach the Integrations API. DISTINCT from the generic workload role, so holding that role alone does not grant connector access.

gateway-client-certificate-id.why: The APIM certificate ENTITY that points at the Key Vault certificate. Not the certificate, and not its thumbprint.

customer-calls-per-day.why: Per-organisation daily request quota, customer audience.

staff-calls-per-day.why: Per-organisation daily request quota, staff audience.

workload-calls-per-day.why: Per-organisation daily request quota, workload audience.
